title: cfd-optical-diagnostics: synthetic shadowgraph, schlieren and BOS rendering from CFD fields
description:
Two complementary ray tracers for predicting what a camera would record looking through a CFD field, plus the detector emulation needed to make a synthetic image comparable to a measurement.

gpuShadow (CUDA) marches rays through a sampled volume, one thread per pixel, using hardware trilinear sampling of the field and its gradient. Three ray-physics modes: sharp (Snell refraction with total internal reflection plus Beer–Lambert attenuation at a resolved interface), eikonal (RK4 march through a graded index, after Sharma et al. 1982), and hybrid. Seven output modes: shadowgraph transmittance, deflection components, classical schlieren via a knife edge at the focal plane, and background-oriented schlieren (BOS) apparent displacement. Finite depth of field is available by thin-lens aperture sampling. A VTK/C++ tracer (ReadSTL) covers the complementary case of a triangulated surface or a single structured-grid volume.

Detector emulation. The rendered deflection field is ground truth, which no experiment can read directly. A processing layer therefore reproduces what a real rig records: a printed (hard-edged) background target, optical point-spread function, shot and read noise, quantisation with independent noise per exposure, and windowed FFT cross-correlation with subpixel Gaussian peak fitting and a loss-of-pairs correction. This makes window-scale smoothing, peak-locking and correlation dropout appear in the synthetic result as they do in a measurement.

Validation and known limits. Each optical path is checked against a closed-form answer rather than against itself: eikonal deflection to 0.19 % on an analytic linear gradient and 7e-4 on a Gaussian phase object; schlieren transmission against the analytic knife-edge relation across sensitivities spanning four orders of magnitude; BOS displacement to ~1.6 %; and recovery of known uniform shifts to better than 0.15 px. Two limitations are documented rather than implied. The shipped interpolant is trilinear (C0), so the refractive-index gradient is discontinuous across cell faces — the intended architecture specifies a tricubic C1 interpolant, and the linear-gradient validation cannot expose the difference because the gradient is constant there by construction. And no result in this release is compared against a measurement: all validation is synthetic against analytic. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md for the full implemented-versus-specified table, and docs/REFERENCES.md for method provenance with DOIs.
